slides.title: Chapter 5: Wallet Recovery
slides.notes: Welcome to chapter five. A wallet is not a bag of coins but a bag of keys, and keys can be lost. Point at the figure from the book and ask what a person would lose if the keys vanished. By the end, one seed written as twelve words brings every key back.
slides.sub: One seed, twelve words, and every key you will ever need back

slides.notes: Seven parts follow one road, and each part opens with a divider. Point at the three counters and tell students that every code example has a twin on the course page. Ask which part they expect to be hardest. The slide numbers let anyone jump back later.
slides.sub: Seven parts; every number is a slide you can jump to
slides.take: Seven parts, and at the end a backup you have actually tested.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers

items: What does a Bitcoin wallet actually contain?
How does a recovery code turn into a seed?
How does one seed make a whole tree of keys?
Which recovery code schemes are in use?
Which derivation paths does a wallet use?
Where does the book differ from the standards?
What must you back up, and how do you test it?

slides.notes: Read the seven questions aloud and promise to return to them in the summary. Ask who can already answer the first one. Most students say a wallet holds coins, and the chapter corrects that. The check-yourself slide at the end uses the same questions.
slides.sub: Seven questions; each one is answered by a part of the deck
slides.take: If you can answer these seven, chapter 5 is yours.

slides.title: Two guesses from 7,002 bitcoin

items.cap: Stefan Thomas, 2015 - Lift Conference, CC BY 2.0

items.who: Stefan Thomas, programmer and former Ripple technology chief; reporter Nathaniel Popper, New York Times.
items.what: Locked out of an IronKey drive that holds the keys to 7,002 BTC; eight of ten password guesses used.
items.when: 2021-01-12 - the story ran; the 7,002 BTC was paid in 2011.
items.where: An IronKey USB drive in a safe, and the front page of the New York Times.
items.why: The password was on a paper he lost; memory was his only backup.
items.how: The drive locks forever after ten wrong guesses. A tested recovery code is the alternative.
cards: In 2011 Stefan Thomas, a programmer and former Ripple technology chief, was paid 7,002 bitcoin and kept the keys on an IronKey USB drive in a safe.
He lost the paper with the password. On 12 January 2021 reporter Nathaniel Popper told the story in the New York Times: eight of ten guesses were already used.
The drive locks forever after ten wrong guesses, and memory was his only backup. A recovery code, tested in advance, is the alternative.

slides.notes: Tell the story slowly. Stefan Thomas was paid 7,002 bitcoin in 2011 and kept the keys on an encrypted drive. Point at the photograph and at the link, and ask what he lacked; a tested backup, not a better memory. Students often blame the drive.
slides.sub: A true story, with real names, dates and places
slides.take: Memory is not a backup; a recovery code you never test is barely one

slides.title: Part 1: Keys in wallets

rows: the file where a wallet keeps its keys and notes
every key made alone, so every key needs a backup
every key follows from one seed by a rule
the one secret all the keys come from
a number added to a key to make a related key
a small computer that signs and never shows its keys

slides.notes: Part one asks what a wallet really holds. Point at the six concepts and read each meaning line once. Ask what the picture on the right shows; the answer is one seed and a rule give every key. A common mistake is to think that a wallet stores coins.
slides.sub: From a bag of keys to one recoverable seed

slides.title: What a wallet really holds
slides.notes: A wallet application prepares a payment, the database supplies keys, a signing device signs, and the network receives it. Point at the four boxes in order. Ask what a wallet with public keys only can still do. It can watch funds but never spend them.
slides.sub: A wallet application, its database, and who signs
slides.take: Keys are the wallet; everything else can be rebuilt from them.

slides.title: Three ways to make keys
slides.notes: Compare the three pictures from the book. Independent keys need one backup each, deterministic keys need one backup, and a hierarchical wallet adds a tree on top. Point at the keys k0 to kn. Ask how many backups the third wallet needs; the answer is only one, the seed.
slides.sub: Loose, deterministic, hierarchical
slides.take: Independent keys: a backup for each. Seed-based keys: one backup.

slides.title: Part 2: Recovery codes

rows: words or characters that stand for the seed
words from a list of 2,048, with a checksum

slides.notes: Part two is about recovery codes, and a code is the seed written for human hands. Point at the six concepts and ask which one is not a recovery code; the brainwallet, because a person chose the words. Students often lump it in with the others.
slides.sub: Seeds written down so a human can keep them

slides.title: Six recovery code schemes

items.name: scheme table
rows: Words from a list of 2,048, a checksum, an optional passphrase
No global word list; a version number inside the code
Two version numbers and a wallet birthday
A non-word code that decrypts the keys in a separate document
One seed split into several codes, for example five made, three needed
Shares made and checked by hand with paper and a pen

slides.notes: Walk down the table one scheme at a time and read only the middle column. BIP39 is the common one, Electrum avoids a global word list, Aezeed carries a wallet birthday and SLIP39 splits a seed. Ask which scheme can be made by hand. Codex32.
slides.sub: What each one adds
slides.take: Same goal, different trade-offs: reliability, privacy, splitting.

slides.title: Why words, and what can go wrong
slides.notes: Four risks sit around a written code. Point at the card about coercion and read the number of attacks aloud. Ask why the book urges writing a code down even though words are easy to remember; the answer is memory fails and people can be forced. A brainwallet is not random.
slides.sub: Memory, imitation and coercion
slides.take: Write it down, make it random, and do not depend on memory.

slides.title: Code 2: Codes check themselves differently

items.name: result table
rows: A checksum over the whole string
Version = the first digits of an HMAC

items.text: codex32 checks by checksum, Electrum by an HMAC prefix.

slides.notes: Different schemes catch typos in different ways. Point at the first row of the result, codex32 valid True, and at the seed number the search found for Electrum. Ask which scheme can be checked by hand. Students are surprised that Electrum marks a seed by a prefix of an HMAC.
slides.sub: codex32 and Electrum, run
slides.take: Every scheme has its own safety net.

slides.title: Code 3: Three of five shares recover the secret

items.text: Any three shares give True; two shares give False.

slides.notes: Secret sharing splits one secret into five shares. Point at the three rows of the result, where any three shares give True and two give False. Ask what two shares reveal; nothing at all. This is a small model and not SLIP39 itself, which works in a different field.
slides.sub: SLIP39's idea, run on a small model
slides.take: Any three recover; two learn nothing.

slides.title: Part 3: The BIP39 stack

rows: the random bits the code is made from
a few bits that reveal a typo
repeated work that makes guessing slow
the stretcher BIP39 uses, and its added string
the 512-bit result that starts the tree

slides.notes: Part three follows BIP39 from random bits to a seed. Point at the six steps in the picture, from entropy to the 512-bit seed. Ask which step makes guessing slow; the answer is the stretch. A common mistake is to think the words themselves are the seed.
slides.sub: Entropy in, twelve words out, then a seed

slides.title: Twelve words between you and 128 bits

items.cap: Trezor One devices - Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0

items.who: Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak (SatoshiLabs, makers of Trezor), with Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe.
items.what: BIP 39: a way to write entropy as ordinary words.
items.where: In the public bips repository on GitHub.
items.how: 2,048 words of eleven bits each, a checksum folded in, and key stretching from words to seed.
cards: Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak of SatoshiLabs, the makers of Trezor, saw that nobody transcribes 128 raw bits correctly. Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe joined them.
On 10 September 2013 they published BIP 39 in the public bips repository on GitHub: a way to write entropy as ordinary words.
The recipe is 2,048 words of eleven bits each, a checksum folded in, and key stretching from the words to the seed.

slides.notes: Tell it as a story of people. Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak built the first hardware signing device and saw that nobody copies 128 bits without errors. Point at the photograph and the link to the standard. Ask why words beat bits; the answer is eleven bits fit one word.
slides.sub: A true story, with real names, dates and places
slides.take: The recovery code is an interface standard between humans and entropy

slides.title: Generating a recovery code
slides.notes: Follow the five steps beside the picture, from entropy and SHA-256 to four checksum bits, twelve pieces of eleven bits and the word list. Point at the 132 bits and ask where the number comes from; 128 plus 4. Students often forget that the checksum is part of the words.
slides.sub: Five steps from random bits to words
slides.take: 12 words x 11 bits = 132 bits = 128 of entropy + 4 of checksum.

slides.title: Code 4: A hash function changes half its bits
slides.notes: Point at the two bars, 126 bits changed and 130 unchanged. Ask what a good hash does when one letter of the input changes. About half of the output bits flip. Students expect a small change to give a small difference, and the chart shows the opposite.
slides.sub: SHA-256, the tool inside BIP39
slides.take: A tiny change makes a huge difference.

slides.title: Code 5: How many words for how much entropy
slides.notes: Point at the bars climbing in equal steps. 128 bits make 12 words and each extra 32 bits add three words. Ask how many words 256 bits need; the answer is twenty-four. The checksum grows too, by one bit for every 32 bits of entropy.
slides.sub: Code length and security strength
slides.take: More bits, more words, more security strength.

slides.title: Code 6: From entropy to twelve words
slides.notes: The chapter's own entropy becomes its own twelve words. Point at the first word, army, and its position 96. Ask why every word is just a number; eleven bits give a position from 0 to 2047 in the list. Students mix up the position with the word.
slides.sub: Eleven-bit segments and the word list
slides.take: Every word is just an eleven-bit number.

slides.title: Code 7: The checksum catches a wrong word

items.name: result table
rows: army van ... media make army (last word changed)

items.text: Right code: checksum True. One word changed: False.

slides.notes: Decode the code back to entropy and check the last four bits. Point at the two rows and at the True and the False. Ask what the checksum catches; the answer is most typos. It cannot repair them, it only warns, and a silent typo becomes a loud error.
slides.sub: BIP39 checksum
slides.take: A checksum turns a silent typo into a loud error.

slides.title: Code 8: Text is normalised before stretching

items.name: result table
rows: as typed: e-acute is one character
after normalising: e plus an accent

items.text: Both spellings give one seed after normalising.

slides.notes: The same word can be stored as one character or as two. Point at the lengths 4 and 5 in the table. Ask why a phone and a laptop could disagree without normalising; the answer is they would build different seeds from the same phrase. Normalising comes before the stretch.
slides.sub: Text normalisation
slides.take: Normalise first, so one phrase gives one seed.

slides.title: Code 9: PBKDF2 stretches the words with a salt

items.name: result table
rows: First 12 hex digits of the result

items.text: Rounds or salt change, and the result is unrelated.

slides.notes: Point at the three results. One round, 2048 rounds and a changed salt give three unrelated outputs. Ask why BIP39 wants 2048 rounds; the answer is each guess becomes slower for an attacker. A different salt gives a different result, which is the same idea as a passphrase.
slides.sub: Key-stretching, salt and the root seed
slides.take: Slow on purpose: 2048 rounds make every guess costly.

slides.title: Code 10: A passphrase opens a different wallet

items.text: Two passphrases give two different wallet addresses.

slides.notes: Same twelve words, two passphrases, two wallets. Point at the two addresses and ask which one holds the funds. Only the one that was funded. This is how a decoy wallet works, and it is also how funds are lost when a passphrase is forgotten.
slides.sub: Optional passphrase in BIP39
slides.take: A passphrase is a second secret to back up.

slides.title: Part 4: The HD wallet

rows: the first private key of the tree
the 32 bytes that let the tree keep growing
a new key from a parent, a chain code and an index
a step only the private parent key can take
a key and its chain code written as one string
which child: 0 to 2^31-1 normal, then hardened

slides.notes: Part four builds the tree of keys. Point at the picture of how the concepts fit. One HMAC of the seed gives the master key and its chain code, and every child comes from a parent, a chain code and an index. Ask what an extended key adds; the answer is the chain code.
slides.sub: One seed, a tree of keys

slides.title: One seed, a tree of keys
slides.notes: The picture is the book's tree. Point at the seed, the master key m and the node m/0/1, since every node is a 32-byte key and a 32-byte chain code. Ask why the tree never runs dry; every child brings a fresh chain code. Paths are the names of the nodes.
slides.sub: Every node is a key and a chain code
slides.take: From one seed grows a tree that backs up as one secret.

slides.title: Code 11: HMAC-SHA512 makes the master key
slides.notes: HMAC-SHA512 gives 64 bytes, and the two halves are the master key and the master chain code. Point at the two halves and at the line that says True True. Ask which half is the key; the answer is the left one. Students often swap the halves.
slides.sub: Master private key and master chain code
slides.take: Half of the HMAC is the key, half the chain code.

slides.title: Code 12: Child keys from a parent and an index

items.text: Each index gives its own key and its own chain code.

slides.notes: Ask for children 0, 1 and 2 and look at the table, where each child gets its own key and its own chain code. Point at the two columns. Ask why the chain code is derived too; it lets the tree keep growing. Three indexes give three unrelated children.
slides.sub: Child key derivation, chain code and index
slides.take: Three indexes, three unrelated children.

slides.title: Code 13: Hardened and normal children differ

items.text: Index 2147483648 is hardened and gives a different key.

slides.notes: Indexes below 2 to the 31 are normal and from there up they are hardened. Point at 2147483648 in the table. Ask what the letter h in a path means; the answer is it adds 2 to the 31 to the index. A hardened child is a different key from child 0.
slides.sub: Hardened child key derivation
slides.take: The letter h in a path is a security decision.

slides.title: Code 14: Why hardened steps protect the parent
slides.notes: Point at the four steps of the leak. The extended public key plus one normal child private key gives the parent private key. Ask why account levels are hardened; the answer is a hardened step cannot be undone this way. The run printed True, which is the bad news.
slides.sub: Using derived child keys
slides.take: Normal child plus xpub exposes the parent; hardening stops it.

slides.title: Code 15: Public keys derived without private keys

items.text: Both routes end at the same public key: True.

slides.notes: Two routes end at the same public key. Point at the box that says True. Ask how a web shop can make addresses without any private key; the answer is it derives public children from the parent public key. Students find it surprising that no secret is needed.
slides.sub: Public child key derivation
slides.take: Public keys alone can make the shop's addresses.

slides.title: Code 16: Extended keys, xprv and xpub

items.text: Both keys are 111 characters; xprv spends, xpub watches.

slides.notes: An extended key is a key plus its chain code written in Base58Check. Point at xprv and xpub, both 111 characters long. Ask which of them can spend; the answer is only xprv. The fingerprint names the key and the depth says how far down the tree it sits.
slides.sub: Extended key encoding and key fingerprint
slides.take: xprv can spend; xpub can only watch.

slides.title: Code 17: 2 to the 31 children, normal and hardened
slides.notes: The book says 2,147,483,647 children and BIP32 says 2 to the 31. Point at the chart, two equal bars. Ask which number is the last index; the answer is 2,147,483,647, one less than the count. Students often treat the last index as the count.
slides.sub: Index numbers for normal and hardened derivation
slides.take: The book's 2,147,483,647 is the last index, not the count.

A key plus a chain code, as xprv or xpub
Numbering doors without holding any key
Public keys derived from a public key
A firewall between parent and child
A step that needs the private parent key
Index numbers for normal and hardened derivation
Two numbered shelves, one ordinary, one locked

slides.notes: The family tree is the main picture and the others follow from it. Point at the two shelves, one for normal children and one for hardened ones. Ask which shelf protects the parent; the answer is the hardened one. Students enjoy finding the picture that fits each section.
slides.sub: Family trees, firewalls and shelves
slides.take: One family tree, with a firewall for hardened children.

slides.title: Part 5: Paths and descriptors

rows: numbers from the master key down to one key
the first number names the scheme; BIP44 fixes five levels
paths fixed by a standard, so not recorded
paths written down next to the recovery code
text that names the script and the keys behind it
the bracket naming a key's parent fingerprint and path

slides.notes: Part five asks which keys a wallet uses. Point at the four steps, from the recovery code to the addresses. A path names a key, standards fix common paths and a descriptor writes script and path down together. Ask what a wallet needs besides the words; the answer is the path.
slides.sub: Which key is which, and how to write it down

slides.title: Code 18: Reading a key path level by level
slides.notes: Read the path m/84h/0h/0h/1/7 level by level. Point at the five levels and at the orange ones, which are hardened. Ask which levels are normal; change and index. A common mistake is to forget that the first three levels carry an h.
slides.sub: HD wallet path, BIP43 and BIP44
slides.take: Purpose, coin, account, change, index.

slides.title: Code 19: Four standard paths, four address types

items.name: result table
rows: First address of the BIP84 test code

items.text: Four purposes give a 1, 3, bc1q and bc1p address.

slides.notes: The function pub turns a path into a public key. Point at the four rows, where purposes 44, 49, 84 and 86 give four kinds of address from one recovery code. Ask which address starts with bc1p; the taproot one, purpose 86. Students expect one code to give one address.
slides.sub: Implicit paths and output scripts
slides.take: One recovery code, four kinds of address.

slides.title: Code 20: Our address equals the standard's own

items.text: Our address equals the published one: True.

slides.notes: To trust a library, compare it with a published answer. Point at the two address rows and at the True, since BIP84 prints the address and Bitcoin Core derives the same one. Ask what you would do if they differed. Stop and find the bug before using any money.
slides.sub: Explicit paths and the standard's test vector
slides.take: Check your code against the published vector.

slides.title: Code 21: A key tweak makes the taproot key

items.name: result table
rows: Output key after the tweak, first 12 hex

items.text: The tweak changes the key; the address shows the new one.

slides.notes: A key tweak adds a number to a key and gives a related key. Point at the two 12-digit prefixes, the internal key and the output key. Ask which one the address encodes; the answer is the tweaked output key. Students expect the internal key.
slides.sub: Key tweak and BIP86
slides.take: Add a number to a key and you get a related key.

slides.title: Implicit and explicit paths

items.name: path table
rows: coin type 1 is testnet in SLIP-0044

slides.notes: Implicit paths are fixed by a standard and explicit paths are written down. Point at the last column of the table and ask why BIP49 shows coin type 1; it is the testnet type in SLIP-0044, a known quirk of the book. Write down every path that is not standard.
slides.sub: Which paths need writing down?
slides.take: Know which paths are implicit and write down the rest.

slides.title: Code 22: A descriptor with its checksum and origin

items.name: result table
rows: A 2-of-3 multisignature descriptor with its checksum

items.text: The checksum and the key origin are computed from the text.

slides.notes: A descriptor is text that names the script and the keys. Point at the eight-character checksum and at the key origin in the bracket. Ask what the three True values mean; the answer is the first three steps are hardened. A two-of-three descriptor gets its own checksum.
slides.sub: Output script descriptors, checksum and key origin
slides.take: One line of text can rebuild the wallet's structure.

slides.title: Multisignature, multipath and miniscript
slides.notes: Multisignature, multipath and miniscript are three ways descriptors grow. Point at the picture, three keys and any two sign. Ask what a multipath descriptor saves; the answer is writing the receiving and change branches only once. Miniscript lets tools analyse a script.
slides.sub: Three ways descriptors grow
slides.take: Descriptors keep the wallet's rules in one line of text.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 5

items.name: analogy table
rows: A street address: country, city, street, house
A list of numbers from the master key to one key
A postal rule: the first number picks the scheme
The purpose number below the master key
A house numbering scheme everyone adopted
Five levels: purpose, coin, account, change, index
A standard everyone knows without being told
A path fixed by a standard, not recorded
The address written on the envelope
A path written down with the backup
A recipe card naming the dish and its ingredients
Text that names the script and the keys

slides.notes: A path is a street address and a descriptor is the whole recipe card. Point at BIP43 and BIP44 and ask which postal rule each one is. The first number picks the scheme, and BIP44 fixes the five levels. Students often confuse the two.
slides.sub: Street addresses and recipe cards
slides.take: A path is a street address; a descriptor is the whole recipe card.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for part 5, the book's sections

items.name: analogy table
rows: Writing the street address down with the key
Paths or descriptors saved with the code
The address of one room in a building
Navigating the HD wallet tree structure
Walking down a family tree by birth order
Levels: purpose, coin, account, change, index

slides.notes: A path is the address of one room in a building, and navigating the tree is walking down the floors. Ask what happens if you keep the key but lose its path. The key may be found but never matched to its room. Write the address down with the key.
slides.sub: Addresses inside a building
slides.take: Write the address down with the key, or the key never finds its room.

slides.title: Part 6: Data that is not keys

rows: a note that names an address or a transaction
a standard file format for exporting labels
payments off the blockchain, with their own state
a one-time backup that helps recover channel funds
readable data turned into data only a key holder reads
the whole database, encrypted by a key from the seed

slides.notes: Part six is about what a recovery code does not hold. Point at the four steps and ask which ones the seed cannot rebuild. Labels, protocol data and the full database. Students assume the seed restores everything, and the next slides show why it does not.
slides.sub: A recovery code is not the whole backup

slides.title: Code 23: Labels exported in the BIP329 format

items.text: One JSON line per label: an address and a transaction.

slides.notes: A label names an address or a transaction. Point at the two JSON lines in the table. BIP329 stores one object per line so any program can read it. Ask what you lose if you lose the labels; the answer is your bookkeeping, not your coins.
slides.sub: Address label, transaction label, BIP329
slides.take: Labels are data too: export them.

slides.title: Channels and encrypted backups
slides.notes: Two answers to data that keys cannot rebuild. Point at the first picture, a static channel backup saved once, which helps but cannot guarantee results. The second picture, an encrypted wallet backup, stores everything with a key from the seed. Ask which one is made often.
slides.sub: Two answers to data that keys cannot rebuild
slides.take: Keys come back from the seed; the rest needs its own copy.

slides.title: The 200,000 BTC in a forgotten wallet file

items.cap: Mt. Gox logo - author unknown, public domain

items.who: Mark Karpeles, chief executive of Mt. Gox; reporter Simon Sharwood, The Register.
items.what: Found about 200,000 BTC in an old-format wallet file.
items.when: 2014-03-21 - three weeks after the bankruptcy filing.
items.where: An old-format wallet file the exchange thought held nothing.
items.why: The company believed its old wallets were empty and had not checked them.
items.how: A file made by software two generations older still held spendable keys.
cards: On 21 March 2014, three weeks after the bankruptcy filing, Mark Karpeles, chief executive of Mt. Gox, said the exchange had found about 200,000 BTC.
Simon Sharwood of The Register reported it. The coins sat in an old-format wallet file that the company believed was empty and had never checked.
A file made by software two generations older still held spendable keys. Wallet files hold keys forever.

slides.notes: Tell it as a story. Mark Karpeles said on 21 March 2014 that Mt. Gox had found about 200,000 bitcoin in an old wallet file. Point at the logo and the link to The Register, and ask why nobody had checked. Backups do not expire, and an untested file is not an empty one.
slides.sub: A true story, with real names, dates and places
slides.take: Wallet files hold keys forever - label, test, and never discard them blindly

slides.title: Part 7: Deploying and testing

items.name: visual: how the concepts fit
rows: 1.  Extended public key on the shop
an xpub placed where it makes addresses
software that turns an xpub into a working shop
how many unused addresses in a row a scan checks
keys kept where no connected computer can read them
the recovery code written on a physical medium
a restore drill before you need it

slides.notes: Part seven puts keys to work. A shop holds only an extended public key and cold storage keeps keys offline, as the four steps show. The chapter ends with the habit that matters most, to test the backup before you need it. Ask who has ever tested one.
slides.sub: Keys at work, and a backup you have tested

slides.title: Code 24: A web shop that holds no private key

items.name: result table
rows: Fresh address made from the xpub

items.text: Three customers get three different addresses.

slides.notes: A shop makes a fresh address per customer from an extended public key. Point at the three addresses. The payment processor does this and never sees a private key. Ask what a hacked server could steal; the answer is no coins, only the list of addresses.
slides.sub: Extended public key on a web store
slides.take: Publish the xpub; the keys never touch the internet.

slides.title: Code 25: The gap limit decides how far a scan looks
slides.notes: Point at the chart, where gaps 5, 10 and 20 find two of the three used keys and only gap 30 finds all three. Ask why a small gap loses key 25; the scan stops after too many unused keys in a row. A scan that stops too early misses your money.
slides.sub: Mind the Gap
slides.take: A scan that stops too early misses your money.

slides.title: Code 26: A digital signature fails if the message changes

items.name: result table
rows: Another message with the same signature

items.text: Verification is True for the signed message only.

slides.notes: A signing device signs the hash of a message. Point at the two rows, True for the signed message and False for another one. Ask what a signature binds; the answer is one key to one message. This is a toy version, and you should never choose the nonce yourself in real life.
slides.sub: Digital signature and the hardware signing device
slides.take: A signature binds one key to one message.

slides.title: Cold storage and the hardware signing device
slides.notes: Cold storage keeps a reserve offline. Follow the four boxes in the picture, from the unsigned transaction to the signed one. Ask where the private key travels; the answer is nowhere. The written backup of the recovery code is the last line of defence, kept apart from the device.
slides.sub: Keep keys where nothing connected can read them
slides.take: Offline keys, a device that signs, and a code on paper.

slides.title: Code 27: The restore drill, a typo opens another wallet

items.name: result table
rows: the code with one word changed

items.text: A single wrong word gives a different wallet: False.

slides.notes: Write down the first address when the wallet is created, then point at the two rows. Restoring from the right code matches, and one wrong word gives a different, empty wallet. Ask why there is no error message; the seed function never judges the words.
slides.sub: Testing a backup
slides.take: Test the restore, not your luck.

slides.title: What a complete backup holds
slides.notes: A complete backup is a list. Read the five items aloud and point at the test step. Ask which item people forget most often; paths and descriptors. A backup is complete only when a restore drill succeeds, not when the list is written.
slides.sub: The chapter's closing list
slides.take: A backup is complete when a restore drill succeeds.

slides.title: Everyday pictures for parts 6 and 7

items.name: analogy table
rows: A sticky note on a drawer

A filing format so notes move between programs
A photocopy of a contract made once
Helps recover channel funds; no guarantee

slides.notes: Labels are sticky notes and a static channel backup is a photocopy. The gap limit is a patient postman who stops after a set number of empty mailboxes. Ask students which part of the backup each picture reminds them of. None of these live in the seed.
slides.sub: Sticky notes, photocopies and mailboxes
slides.take: Notes, copies and mailboxes: each needs its own backup or setting.

slides.title: Check yourself

items.name: question table
rows: Why is one seed better than many loose keys?
How many words does 256 bits of entropy make?
What does the checksum protect against?
Why does a passphrase change the wallet?
How do you know a backup works?

slides.notes: Try each question aloud before you look at the slide. If you hesitate, go back to the code slide named on the right. Ask students to pair up and quiz each other. These are the questions the exam will build on, so answer without looking.
slides.sub: Six questions, then the slides that answer them
slides.take: Answer without looking, then check the code slide.

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.notes: Five lines carry the chapter. Read one per part and ask students to name its code slide. Wallets derive keys from a seed, a code is entropy in words, a seed is stretched slowly, the tree hands every purpose a key, and a backup counts only once restored.
slides.sub: One line per part
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, its part's code slides carry the receipt.

slides.title: Where to go from here

groups.head: Seminal work
rows: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System

slides.notes: These are the places to read, check and ask. Point at the Standards group and the three BIPs first. Use the tools only offline, and never type a real recovery code into a website. The course page holds the same code in the same order as the slides.
slides.sub: Every entry is a live link; the course page holds the same code
slides.take: Twelve words on paper beat every password you have ever memorised.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say

items: Why one seed replaced bags of keys
What twelve words carry and how they become a tree
Which path your wallet walks, and who else can walk it
What a tested backup is

slides.notes: Read the four outcomes aloud and ask each student which one they could not yet say. Send them back to the matching part of the deck. A tested backup is the outcome most often skipped. Questions are welcome.
slides.sub: And where each claim gets its proof
